units.t: Investing. Episode two.
In this episode: Bonds explained, Diversification, Index funds and ETFs and Property investing in Australia.
Part one. Bonds explained.
Governments and companies borrow trillions of dollars from investors.
Bonds are how, and they quietly shape your super and your mortgage.
A loan you can buy.
When you buy a bond, you are lending money.
The borrower, called the issuer, promises to pay regular interest, known as the coupon, and to repay the original amount, called the face value, on a set maturity date.
A five-year bond with a $100 face value and a 4% coupon pays $4 a year, usually in instalments, then returns the $100 at the end.
Shares make you a part-owner of a company; bonds make you a lender.
Lenders get paid before shareholders, which is part of why bonds are generally less risky.
Safe and not so safe.
The Australian Government borrows by issuing Treasury bonds through the Australian Office of Financial Management, and states borrow through agencies such as NSW Treasury Corporation.
A national government that borrows in its own currency can tax and has a central bank, so the chance it fails to repay is considered very low.
Australia has held a AAA credit rating from all three major agencies for many years.
Companies can fail, so investors want extra interest to cover credit risk, the chance of default.
Bonds rated BBB- or above are investment grade.
Lower-rated 'junk' bonds pay more because the risk is genuinely higher.
A higher rate is a price for extra risk, not a free bonus.
The bond see-saw.
Bonds can be sold before maturity, and their prices change.
Imagine you hold a bond paying 3% a year.
Then interest rates rise and new bonds pay 5%.
Nobody will pay full price for your 3% bond when they can get 5% elsewhere, so its market price falls until its effective return, called its yield, matches the new rate.
The reverse happens when rates fall.
This see-saw is the most important idea in bond investing.
The longer a bond has left until maturity, the more its price moves when rates change.
When bonds hurt.
Bonds are called defensive, but they can lose value.
In 2022, central banks raised interest rates quickly to fight high inflation.
Because bond prices fall when rates rise, many bond funds lost money, in some markets in their worst year in generations.
Unusually, shares fell at the same time, so balanced portfolios had few places to hide.
Inflation is another danger: a fixed 3% coupon buys less each year if prices rise 6%.
If you hold a high-quality bond to maturity, though, you still receive the face value back.
Term deposits differ.
An Australian bank deposit is covered by the Financial Claims Scheme up to $250,000 per person per institution and doesn't fluctuate.
A bond sells for whatever it fetches that day, and bond funds never mature, so their value moves with rates.
Bonds in your super.
Most diversified portfolios, including many super options, hold shares and bonds.
Bonds provide predictable income and usually swing far less than shares.
High-quality government bonds have often held their value or risen during share crashes, though 2022 showed this isn't guaranteed.
Older investors, and anyone needing money within a few years, typically hold more bonds and cash.
Check your fund's split between growth and defensive assets.
When rates rise, the bond portion may dip, but new bonds pay better yields.
Be cautious of offers promising well above market rates; that return reflects extra risk.
This is general information only.
See a licensed financial adviser for personal advice, and Moneysmart for independent guides.
The key idea: A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays you interest and returns your money at a set date.
Part two. Diversification.
It's sometimes called the only free lunch in investing: a way to reduce risk without necessarily giving up return.
Eggs and baskets.
The old saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' is the heart of diversification.
If you invest everything in one company and it collapses, you can lose everything.
Spread the same money across 200 companies, and one collapse costs you only a small slice.
Even household names can go bust or shrink dramatically.
Diversification doesn't prevent losses when the whole market falls.
But it greatly reduces the damage from any one bad bet, which is the kind of loss that is hardest to recover from.
Why it works.
Investments don't all move together.
If one company is hit by a scandal, another may be having a great year.
Combine many different assets and their ups and downs partly offset each other, so the portfolio swings less than its parts.
Harry Markowitz formalised this in 1952, later earning a Nobel Prize, and the line that diversification is 'the only free lunch in finance' is often attributed to him.
Correlation runs from +1 to -1.
At +1 two investments move in lockstep, so holding both adds no diversification.
Zero means unrelated; negative means one tends to rise when the other falls.
One catch: in severe crises, correlations between risky assets often rise, just when you want them low.
Across asset classes.
The biggest decision in most portfolios is the mix of asset classes, often called asset allocation.
Shares offer growth but can fall sharply.
Bonds and cash are steadier and have often held up better when shares slump.
Property behaves differently again.
A 'balanced' super option might hold roughly two-thirds in growth assets and the rest in defensive assets, although definitions vary between funds.
Many researchers argue that asset allocation explains most of the ups and downs in a diversified portfolio over time, more than which individual shares are picked.
Sectors and borders.
Our share market is unusually lopsided.
Financials, especially the big banks, and materials, especially miners, make up a large share of the main index.
Technology and healthcare are much smaller than in global markets.
Owning four big banks gives little diversification, because they tend to move together.
An investor with only Australian shares is heavily exposed to banks, iron ore and the housing market.
Australia is only around 2% of global share markets, yet many Australians hold mostly local shares.
This home bias is partly familiarity and partly franking credits.
Global shares bring new industries, economies and currency risk: when the Australian dollar rises, overseas investments are worth less in local terms.
Some funds 'hedge' to reduce this.
Hidden concentration.
Enron, the US energy company, collapsed in 2001.
Many employees had much of their retirement savings in its shares, so they lost their jobs and savings together.
Your job, home and super may also depend on the same local economy.
Another trap is 'diworsification': ten funds that all hold the same large companies look diversified but aren't.
Check what lies under the labels, and look for one company, sector, country or property making up most of your wealth.
A broad index fund or diversified super option can hold hundreds or thousands of investments at low cost.
Diversification reduces risk but cannot eliminate it.
This is general information only; see a licensed adviser, and Moneysmart for independent tools.
The key idea: Diversification means spreading your money across many investments so no single failure can sink you.
Part three. Index funds and ETFs.
The boring, low-cost way to invest that beats most professional fund managers over time.
Owning the market.
Most investment funds are actively managed: professionals try to pick shares that will beat the market.
An index fund does something simpler.
It buys every company in a market index, like the ASX 200 or the S and P 500, in proportion to its size, and just holds them.
You don't try to beat the market; you are the market.
The first index fund for ordinary investors was launched in 1976 by John Bogle, founder of Vanguard.
Critics called it 'Bogle's folly'.
It turned out to change investing.
Why passive often wins.
It seems obvious that experts should beat a fund that simply buys everything.
But studies such as S and P's SPIVA reports find that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index over 10 to 15 years, once fees are counted.
Before costs, the average investor earns the market return, so after higher costs, the average active investor must do worse.
It's also very hard to identify in advance which managers will be the lucky few who win.
In 2007, Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S and P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years.
By the end of 2017, the index fund averaged about 7% a year, the hedge funds about 2%.
Fees compound.
Index funds are cheap because they don't pay teams of analysts to pick stocks.
Broad index funds and ETFs often charge between about 0.
3% a year, while active funds commonly charge 1% or more.
That gap looks small, but it is taken from your balance every year, whether markets rise or fall.
On a $100,000 investment over 30 years, earning 6% a year after fees instead of 7% leaves you with about $187,000 less.
You can't control market returns, but you can control costs.
Check the fee on any fund before you buy it, since it is one of the few numbers you can know in advance.
ETFs and going global.
An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, is bought and sold on the stock exchange like a share.
Many track an index, so one unit gives you a slice of hundreds or thousands of companies.
You can buy them through any online broker, often with small amounts.
There are ETFs for Australian shares, global shares, bonds, property and more.
Some are narrow or complex, like those chasing a single theme or using leverage; broad, simple ones suit most long-term investors.
Australian shares make up only about 2% of world markets, and the ASX is dominated by banks and miners.
Global funds add diversification and industries like technology that are smaller here.
Some ETFs hold a mix of shares and bonds in one fund, rebalancing automatically.
Time, not timing.
Nobody reliably predicts short-term market moves, and some of the best days often come shortly after the worst, so jumping in and out can mean missing the recovery.
Many investors use dollar-cost averaging: investing a fixed amount regularly, which buys more units when prices are low and fewer when they're high.
Time in the market beats timing the market.
Shares suit money you won't need for at least five to seven years, because markets can fall sharply in the short term.
First build an emergency fund and clear high-interest debt.
Your super is probably already invested in shares.
This is general information; ASIC's Moneysmart has free guides, and a licensed adviser can help.
The key idea: An index fund buys every company in an index in proportion to its size, rather than trying to pick winners.
Part four. Property investing in Australia.
Australians love bricks and mortar.
Here is how investment property actually makes, and loses, money.
Why property looms large.
Residential real estate is the largest single component of Australian household wealth, worth far more in total than the Australian share market.
Around two million Australians own at least one investment property, according to tax statistics, and most own just one.
Its appeal is easy to see: it is tangible, familiar and can be bought largely with borrowed money.
But an investment property is a business decision, not a home, and it should be judged on its numbers, costs and risks like any other investment.
Returns and hidden costs.
Rental yield is annual rent divided by price.
A $750,000 unit rented for $600 a week earns about $31,200 a year, a gross yield of roughly 4.
Net yield subtracts costs and is always lower.
The second return is capital growth, which is never guaranteed and varies by location and period.
Yields in many cities have been modest, so investors have leaned on growth.
Costs add up.
Stamp duty, a state purchase tax, can run to tens of thousands of dollars.
Then come legal and inspection costs, loan interest, rates, landlord insurance, strata fees, repairs, management fees and, in some states, land tax, plus vacancies.
Selling brings agent fees and possibly capital gains tax.
A property can rise in value and still disappoint.
Gearing and leverage.
Most property investors borrow, often most of the purchase price.
This is gearing, or leverage.
Suppose you buy a $600,000 property with a $120,000 deposit and a loan for the rest.
If the property rises 10%, it gains $60,000, which is 50% of your own money.
If it falls 10%, you lose $60,000, half your deposit, and still owe the full loan.
Leverage magnifies outcomes in both directions.
You must also keep making repayments whether or not the property is tenanted, and if interest rates rise, those repayments can climb quickly.
Negative gearing and tax.
A property is positively geared when rent exceeds costs, including interest, and negatively geared when costs exceed rent.
That loss has generally been deductible against other income, such as wages.
Legislation passed in June 2026 narrows this: from 1 July 2027, losses on established homes bought after 7:30 pm AEST on 12 May 2026 can only be offset against residential property income and gains.
Earlier purchases and new builds keep the old treatment.
A deduction only recovers part of a loss.
Capital gains tax applies when you sell an investment property.
The 50% discount for assets held over 12 months is being replaced from 1 July 2027 by indexing the cost base for inflation, with a 30% minimum tax; gains built up before then keep the discount.
Use ATO guidance and a registered tax agent.
Concentration and checks.
Property prices can fall, as they have in some Australian cities and in mining towns after booms faded.
One property often represents a huge share of an investor's wealth: one asset, one suburb, one market.
It is illiquid, since selling takes weeks or months and costs a lot.
Rate rises, a long vacancy or a major repair can strain your budget.
Calculate net yield using realistic costs, not brochure figures.
Could you cope with rates two or three percentage points higher, or three months without rent?
Be wary of spruikers and 'free' property packages that earn developer commissions; ASIC has warned about them.
This is general information only.
Speak with a licensed adviser and registered tax agent, and see Moneysmart.
The key idea: Residential property is the biggest store of household wealth in Australia, but an investment property is a business decision.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What are you doing when you buy a bond?
Answer. Lending money to the issuer for interest.
Question two. What is the main purpose of diversification?
Answer. To limit the harm from any one bad investment.
Question three. What does an index fund do?
Answer. Holds all the companies in an index.
Question four. What is the best way to view an investment property?
Answer. As a business judged on numbers and risks.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
